title: Chapter 192 – The Stillborn Roll
html:
[The Roll Room, Lin Clan Hall – Cheng Hui]

Cheng Hui has never been inside a library, and the Roll Room frightens him more than the Bloom.

It is a long low chamber at the back of the clan hall, with a floor of worn brick and a ceiling of smoke-darkened beams. Shelves run along both walls from floor to rafters, crowded with scroll cases and bound ledgers and boxes of loose slips tied with string. A single high window lets in a bar of morning light. In it, dust turns. The air smells of paper, tallow, and a century of damp.

"It is only a room," says Zhao, from the desk at the far end.

"I know."

"You are standing in the door like a man about to be hanged."

"I know that too."

Zhao looks up from his ledger. He is a narrow, stooped man, the clan's accountant by habit and its steward by necessity, with ink on three fingers and a face worn thin by the Night of Counting. In the last month he has lost a hand's breadth of belt and gained a whole population of orphans. He does not smile, but something in his eyes eases.

"Come in," he says. "Sit. I will not make you read anything you do not wish to."

Cheng Hui sits. The stool is too low for him. He is nineteen and the eldest of the Seven, and the Hall's careful food has made him tall without making him wide; he folds up on it like a heron. The other six crowd in behind him and settle along the wall on crates, the way they always do: Duan Ke with his arms crossed, Hai Ren perched, Zhen Li biting her nails. Little Tao has fallen asleep against Mo Yan's shoulder. Ao has been left in the kitchen with Qinghe. Three is too young to be asked this.

"You wanted to see the Roll," says Zhao. "Why?"

Cheng Hui has rehearsed an answer. He opens his mouth and finds he has forgotten it.

"Because Jian said the Gate burned names," he says. "He said every life was a coin. He said the Nine fed it with people."

"Yes."

"And Ethan told us we were made. That we were patterns he wrote and grew in the dark. That we are..." He stops. The word is an ugly one. "Copies."

"I have heard the phrase."

"Then where did the first one come from?" The question rushes out of him, louder than he means. "You cannot make a copy of nothing. A pattern has to be of someone. If the Gate burned names, then somebody had a name, and somebody lost it. I want to know whose."

For a long moment Zhao does not answer. The bar of light has crept an inch along the desk. Outside, a child shouts, and a woman's voice calls her in.

"Cheng Hui," says Zhao. "Do you know what is in the left-hand cases?"

"No."

"The Stillborn Roll."

* * *

Cheng Hui thinks, as Zhao climbs the stepladder, about how he came to this room at all.

It was Kuang's idea. The boy is thirteen, newly named heir, and fiercely serious about it; he found Cheng Hui in the kitchen two nights ago, sitting alone over a cold bowl, and said without preamble: "Zhao says the Roll has nineteen hundred and four names in it now. Do you want to be in it?"

"I'm not a Lin."

"You live at my aunt's table," said Kuang, with the unanswerable logic of thirteen. "You eat our barley. You've been teaching my cousins to read. If you're not a Lin, I do not know what the word is for."

Cheng Hui had not slept that night. He had lain in the dark with Tao's small warm back against his side, listening to the Hall breathe, and thought: what am I? A pattern. A mistake. A boy who woke in a bed one morning with a head full of someone else's memory of a childhood he could not have had. He had been told, kindly, by an old man made of light, that he was made. He had believed it, because it was easier than the alternative, which was that he did not know.

Now the stepladder creaks, and the lacquer box comes down, and his hands begin to shake.

It is not a large thing, as books go.

It is a stack of eleven narrow ledgers bound in black cloth, each a hand's breadth thick, kept in a lacquer box on the highest shelf and brought down by Zhao on a stepladder with an unexpected tenderness. He sets the box on the desk and does not open it. Cheng Hui sees that the lacquer is worn pale where a thumb has rested.

"Every clan keeps one," says Zhao. "The births are in the Roll of the Living. The deaths are in the Roll of the Gone. But there is a third roll, and it is the smallest, and nobody likes to read it. It is for the children who were never named."

"Stillborn."

"And the very young. Those who die before the third day. By custom they are not given a milk name, because a name is a hold on the world, and an unnamed child is thought to have none. They are entered in black ink, with the date and the mother's line, and nothing else." He lays his hand flat on the lid. "I have been Steward for forty years. In forty years, I have entered fourteen."

Cheng Hui swallows. "And in the other ledgers?"

"Four hundred and eleven. Going back to the Founding." Zhao's voice is level, but his hand tightens. "The Hall of the Sixth Door was built the year after the Founders' Bell. The oldest ledger begins in that year."

Nobody on the crates is moving.

"Open it," says Cheng Hui.

* * *

The first ledger smells of age and iron gall.

The paper is thick, like cloth, and the ink has gone from black to the brown of dried blood. Zhao turns the pages with a clerk's careful fingers. The entries are short. They are all the same.

Year 3. Third month. A girl, to the line of Lin Wei-ran. Born still.

Year 3. Ninth month. A boy, to the line of Lin Shu. Born still.

Year 4. Second month. A boy, to the line of Lin Wei-ran. Not breathing.

Cheng Hui reads them aloud, because Zhao has asked him to, and by the tenth he has stopped hearing the words. They are only a rhythm: a girl, a boy, a boy, a girl. Behind him, someone is breathing very quickly.

"Stop," says Duan Ke.

Zhao stops.

"Go back." Duan Ke has come off his crate. He is sixteen and wiry, with a scar through one eyebrow that he got from a fall he does not remember, and he is looking at the page with an expression Cheng Hui has never seen him wear. "That one. The seventh from the top."

Zhao turns back. His finger rests on the line.

Year 11. Fifth month. A boy, to the line of Lin Shu. Born with the cord around the neck. Taken from the mother's room before the dawn watch.

"Taken," says Duan Ke.

"It is a custom," says Zhao slowly. "The body is removed so that the mother does not..." He stops. "No. That is the phrase for burial. The phrase for burial is carried out. Taken is something else."

"What is it?"

"I do not know." Zhao's face has gone the color of the paper. "I have never seen it before."

He turns the page. And the next. And Cheng Hui, who is watching the old man's hands, sees them begin to shake.

The word recurs. It is not on every line. It is on one in nine, scattered through the years, and each time it is set in the same small, careful hand, a hand that is not the Steward's. Taken from the room before the dawn watch. Taken by the midwife and not returned. Taken, and a lamp seen in the cellar.

A lamp in the cellar.

"The basement," says Hai Ren, very softly. "He said the first Gate was a basement closet."

"This is not his world," says Cheng Hui. "This is the valley."

"The valley has cellars."

"It has no..."

He cannot finish. The bar of light has reached the edge of the ledger and lies across the page like a blade, and in it he can see the last entry on the open leaf, which is the one that Zhao has just turned to, and which Zhao is not reading aloud.

* * *

Year 88. Eleventh month. A boy, to the line of Lin Shu. Alive at birth. Taken by the Warden of the Hall at the mother's asking. Named Cheng Hui in the Hall's book.

He reads it twice.

Then he reads it again, slowly, with his lips moving, as if the words were in a language he had half learned.

"It says," he says. His voice is thin and strange. "It says that I..."

"Cheng Hui."

"It says I was born." He looks up. Zhao is standing. The old man has taken a step toward him, and his ink-stained hand is half lifted, as if to catch something falling. "Not made. Born. In this valley. To a mother of the clan. In the Year 88."

"Yes."

"And the Warden took me."

"The Warden of the Hall. At the mother's asking." Zhao's throat works. "Cheng Hui, I think... I think there was a reason, and it was not a cruel one. There is a line further down, in the margin. In the same hand."

Cheng Hui bends to look. The margin is crowded with tiny script, faded almost to nothing. He has to hold the page close to read it.

She asked that he be kept. The Hall could keep him. The blood fault does not run in the clan, but the child had the tremor from the first breath. I have not told her of the Gate. I have told her he will sleep.

I do not know whether I have done right.

"The blood fault," says Zhao. "Your hands."

Cheng Hui looks at his own hands. They are long, and pale, and they have trembled since he can remember, a fine fast shake he has learned to hide in his sleeves. He had thought it was fear. Ethan Cole's daughter had the same fault, the same quiver in the fingers, the same slow wasting of the blood. He had heard it in the Hall's records. He had never once thought of it as his.

"Mei's sickness," he says.

"It was in the valley before the Hall," says Zhao. "It has been in some of our children for six hundred years. We always called it the tremor. We never knew it had a name."

* * *

They go through the ledgers all morning.

It does not take long, once they know what to look for. Zhao reads, and Cheng Hui writes, and the others hover in the rows between the shelves with the stricken, hungry look of people who have been hungry for a long time without knowing it. Hai Ren finds her own: Year 97, a girl to the line of Lin Wei-ran, taken. Zhen Li finds hers. Tao finds his, with Mo Yan's help, a small line in a small hand at the bottom of the nineteenth leaf: Year 112, a boy, born with the tremor and a cleft in the lip. His mother wept. I have said the Hall will keep him whole.

Duan Ke finds his own and walks out of the room.

He comes back an hour later with snow in his hair and his eyes red. He says nothing. He sits on his crate and picks up a scroll case and begins to read, with the stubborn grim attention of a boy who has decided that if he looks hard enough at a thing, it cannot hurt him.

There are seven names on the list. Seven, in six hundred years. Seven children of the Lin clan, taken from their mothers' rooms by the Warden of the Hall: seven, and one more.

"Mo Yan," says Zhao.

She lifts her head from Tao's hair. She does not speak, because she does not, but she looks at the old man with her gray eyes wide, and he answers the look as if she had asked.

"You were born in the winter of the Year 301. To the line of Lin Shu." The old man's mouth works. "Your mother's milk name was Hua. She is in the Roll of the Gone. She died the following spring. The entry says, in a different hand, that she was found at the foot of the Founders' Wall, and that she did not seem to have been ill."

Mo Yan looks at him a long time.

Then she puts her hand to her heart, and nods, once, slowly. I knew, it says. Not the name. But I knew there was a someone.

Cheng Hui looks away. He has to.

* * *

"It does not make sense," says Hai Ren.

It is past noon. They have eaten bread in the Roll Room, quietly, off the corner of the desk, and nobody has quite looked at anyone else. The bar of light has moved to the far wall. Hai Ren is fourteen, and sharp, and reads faster than any of them; she has a stack of slips on her knee and a deep line between her brows.

"Say it," says Cheng Hui.

"The Warden took us. Seven children, over six hundred years. Not for the Gate. The Gate wants names, not infants." She holds up a slip. "They were sick. Every one of us had the tremor. Every one. And the Warden's note says kept. It says kept whole."

"He fed the Gate," says Duan Ke harshly. "That is what Ethan said."

"Did he?" Hai Ren turns her head. "Or did he say the Gate was fed with names? A name is a hold on the world. These children were never given milk names. They were entered in black, unnamed, and then taken." She sets the slip down carefully. "The Gate could not have burned them. They had no names to burn."

Nobody moves.

"Then what did the Warden do with us?"

"What did he say he would do?" says Zhao softly. "I have told her he will sleep."

"He put us in the beds," says Zhen Li.

"In the Hall."

"In the oldest ring." Zhen Li's face is white. "Before the experiments. Before Ethan's patterns. The first-ring sleepers, the four hundred and twelve..." She stops. "The lamps. The ones that went out last night."

Cheng Hui goes cold.

It comes in a rush, the way a thing falls into place when you have been staring at it from the wrong side. He sees the Hall's great vault as Jian described it: ring on ring of lamps, each a sleeper, and the oldest at the top. He sees the Operator program Ethan spoke of, the eight experiments, the seven put to sleep. He has always understood that the Seven were the survivors.

But Ethan did not make the Seven in a basement. The Seven were children of this valley, sick children, brought by their mothers to the only place that had ever promised a cure. And the Warden of the Hall, who knew what the Gate had cost, had not been able to bear the cost of a child's death without a try.

"He didn't make us," says Cheng Hui. "He saved us."

"Or he thought he did."

"There's a difference?"

"There always is." Zhao takes the ledger from him and closes it with great gentleness. "That is what a Steward learns. A child kept is not a child living. But a child lost is not a child saved, either. It is only a child who is not here to be asked."

* * *

Hai Ren is the one who says what no one else will.

"My mother," she says. She is holding the slip for Year 97, and her voice is flat, the way a person's is when they are afraid of what it will do if it moves. "She gave me up. She let him take me. She knew I would not be coming back for six hundred years."

"She did not know that," says Zhao.

"She knew I was gone."

"Yes."

"Then how can I be a Lin?" She looks up, and her eyes are fierce and wet. "How can I belong to a family that let me go?"

Zhao is silent for a long moment. He takes off his spectacles and wipes them on his sleeve, slowly, a clerk stalling for time. When he speaks, it is in the voice he uses for the Roll, the dry exact voice of a man who has spent forty years keeping the count.

"I have written eleven hundred deaths in this ledger in the last month," he says. "I have written them in the Gone. And in each of them, in the margin, there is a name I could not stop myself writing, the name of the person who loved them most. Do you know why?"

"No."

"Because a clan is not who stays," says Zhao. "A clan is who is written down by someone who could not bear to leave them out."

Hai Ren stares at him. Then, very slowly, she lowers the slip.

It is Tao who says it, in the end.

He is the smallest, and has been quiet all day, curled up on Mo Yan's lap with his thumb in his mouth. He takes it out now and says, in a perfectly clear voice, "Then the Hall isn't a place where we were made. It's a place where we were left."

A silence.

"They left us," says Tao, "because they didn't know what else to do. And it was wrong. But they meant to come back."

Cheng Hui looks at him. The boy's eyes are enormous and solemn, a child's eyes in a face that has been through six hundred years, and he sees, as if from a great distance, what is being offered him.

It is a name.

Not a milk name. Not a pattern's tag. A name, in the Roll of the Living, in good black ink, with the date of his birth and the line of his mother. A place in the world that is not a bed in a hall or a seat at a kitchen table. A claim on a clan, and a clan's claim on him.

"Zhao," he says.

"Yes."

"If we asked. If the Seven asked to be entered." He struggles to find the words. "In the Living. As Lin. As what we were."

"You would be Lin," says Zhao. "By blood. By the Roll. By six hundred years of ink."

"Would they let us?"

"The Head would. I think the clan would." The old man's voice trembles. "I think Elder Mu, if she were here, would weep."

"And Jian?"

"Your cousin," says Zhao, with a wan little smile, "would very probably fall over."

Cheng Hui laughs. It comes out cracked. It is the first laugh he has had in a month. Around him the others are laughing too, in that helpless sniffling way, Hai Ren with her face in her hands, Duan Ke slapping the crate, little Tao asking what is funny and nobody able to tell him.

Then Mo Yan stands.

She puts down the sleeping boy, carefully, on the crate. She crosses the brick floor to the desk and takes up the pen in her thin small hand. She dips it in the ink. She turns to the empty page at the end of the Roll of the Living and writes, in a clear childish script, one line:

Lin Mo Yan. Born Year 301, winter. Returned.

She sets down the pen and looks at them, and her face is shining.

* * *

Zhao writes the entries himself, one at a time, in his small exact hand.

Lin Cheng Hui. Born Year 88, to the line of Lin Shu. Returned. He blows on the ink. Lin Duan Ke. Lin Hai Ren. Lin Zhen Li. Each name goes down in black, in the Roll of the Living, below the nineteen hundred and four he has already counted. Each time the pen lifts, a small sound passes through the room, not quite a sigh and not quite a sob, the sound of a held breath being let go.

When he reaches Tao's line, the boy wakes and climbs onto the desk to watch. "Is that me?" he asks, pointing at the wet ink.

"That is you."

"It's very black."

"It will dry," says Zhao gravely. "It will last longer than the paper."

Tao considers this with enormous care. Then he reaches out one finger and touches the edge of the letters, leaving a tiny smudge, and nods as if a contract had been signed.

Cheng Hui watches the smudge and thinks that he has never seen anything so beautiful in his life.

It is Cheng Hui who sees the second thing.

He is leaning over her shoulder to read what she has written, and the light from the high window falls across the facing page, the one that Zhao turned over in his haste at the start and never looked back at. It is the end leaf of the oldest ledger, the one that begins in Year 3. It is blank except for a single entry at the very bottom, in the same careful hand that wrote kept whole.

It is not a birth. It is not a death. It is a note of three lines, and it is not in black ink but in red.

The Nine have agreed that the Rest of All shall not be woken save by the consent of the Nine. I have signed for the Sixth. If any of the Nine is lost, let the Roll provide a successor of her own blood, born in the valley, who knows the cost.

I have chosen eight. They do not know it. Heaven forgive me.

—Warden of the Hall, Year 3.

Cheng Hui reads it. And reads it again.

The room has gone entirely quiet. He is aware of Zhao behind him, not breathing. He is aware of the child beside him, her pen frozen above the ink.

I have chosen eight.

"It was not Ethan," he says. His voice is a whisper. "It was never Ethan who picked us. The Warden picked us, six hundred years ago. He put us in the beds. He knew there would be a day when the Nine would need to be nine again."

"A successor," says Hai Ren. "Of her own blood."

"Of the valley's blood." Cheng Hui lifts his head, and for the first time in his life, he is not afraid. "We aren't copies. We're what was left of the clan the Hall promised to keep. We're heirs."

He looks at the seven faces around him, and the one asleep, and the old man behind them with the ledger in his arms. He looks at the red ink, at its dried-blood brown, at the name signed beneath it that he cannot read, because the signature has been scratched out. Someone, long ago, did not want it known who had made the choice.

"Somebody tried to hide this," he says.

"Yes."

"Who?"

Zhao does not answer. His gaze has gone past Cheng Hui, past the shelves, to the narrow door at the far end of the Roll Room. It is the door through which, an hour ago, no one had come. It stands open now.

In it, silent as a cat, with a hand wrapped in white cloth and a veil of gray gauze across her face, a woman is standing.

"Do not trouble yourselves," says the Veiled, in a pleasant, tired voice. "It was I who scratched it out. I have been wondering how long it would take you to find it."
